title: Non-Cyclic (ZMod n)ˣ: 2-Torsion Bound and Wilson's Theorem
description: Proves: for n ≥ 3, if (ZMod n)ˣ is non-cyclic then there exists x with x² = 1, x ≠ ±1. Builds infrastructure for units of ZMod n and characterizes when Wilson's product has extra square roots of unity. 9 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p) for prime p. For composite n, (n-1)! ≡ 0 (mod n). The cyclic structure of (ZMod n)ˣ (cyclic iff n = 1, 2, 4, p^k, or 2p^k) determines whether -1 is the 'only' primitive element.
overview.problemStatement: Prove: if (ZMod n)ˣ is non-cyclic then there exists x: ZMod n with x² = 1 and x ≠ ±1.
overview.proofStrategy: A non-cyclic group has more than 2 solutions to x² = 1 (since cyclic groups of even order have exactly 2). The extra solutions are units x ≠ ±1 with x² = 1. Lift from ZMod n to (ZMod n)ˣ.
keyInsights: **Cyclic vs. non-cyclic**: (ZMod n)ˣ is cyclic iff n ∈ {1, 2, 4, p^k, 2p^k} for odd prime p. Non-cyclic n (e.g., n = 8, 15, 24) have extra x with x² = 1.
**2-torsion count**: in a cyclic group of even order, the 2-torsion subgroup has exactly 2 elements (±1). Non-cyclic means more 2-torsion.
**Wilson product**: for composite n, Wilson's product changes from -1 to 0 or other values depending on the structure of (ZMod n)ˣ.

conclusion.summary: 9 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms. Non-cyclic (ZMod n)ˣ implies existence of extra square roots of unity beyond ±1.
conclusion.implications: This result explains why Wilson's theorem (product of units = -1) only holds for primes and prime powers: for other n, the extra 2-torsion elements make the product ≠ -1.
openQuestions: Can Wilson's theorem be generalized to characterize all n with Π(ZMod n)ˣ = -1?
Can the structure of (ZMod n)ˣ be fully classified in Lean?
Can the non-cyclic condition be characterized arithmetically (in terms of n)?
